<explanation>
Based on our analysis of the file structure and the README, Mythic is a complex, multi-container, full-stack red teaming framework with both a backend (largely written in Go, with components for authentication, database management, RabbitMQ interactions, etc.) and a frontend (a React UI named MythicReactUI). It incorporates multiple Docker containers (for the Go services, React UI, databases like PostgreSQL, RabbitMQ messaging, Hasura, nginx reverse proxies, and additional services for monitoring and dashboards) orchestrated via docker-compose. There is also a CLI (Mythic_CLI) that manages the installation, update, and overall startup process that ties together the individual container components.

Below is a set of detailed guidelines on how to create an accurate system design diagram/architecture overview for this project:

1. Identify and label the main components:
   • Frontend/UI: Represent “MythicReactUI” (the browser-based interface built with React) as one box.
   • Backend Services: Represent the “mythic-docker” component – including authentication, API controllers (the webserver controllers in Go), database connectors, and microservices. Make sure to indicate the authentication middleware, the event processing (eventing, RabbitMQ interaction), and file/database services.
   • CLI Orchestrator: Show “Mythic_CLI” as a control component that issues commands (e.g., installing agents, managing Docker containers, updating configuration) and initiates startup.
   • Messaging and Integration: Include the RabbitMQ container/services with both sending and receiving channels for tasking, eventing, and RPC messages.
   • Data Storage: Incorporate the PostgreSQL container (postgres-docker) and Hasura (hasura-docker) for database management and real-time GraphQL APIs.
   • Supporting Infrastructure: Depict additional supporting containers such as nginx (for reverse proxying), Grafana (for dashboards/monitoring), Prometheus (metrics), and other Docker-based integrations.

2. Define the relationships and data flow:
   • Use directional arrows to denote API calls from the frontend (MythicReactUI) to the backend webserver.
   • Show that the CLI tool (Mythic_CLI) sends commands that start/shutdown/update the various containers.
   • Illustrate how backend services communicate with RabbitMQ to exchange asynchronous messages for tasking and events (with separate channels for pushing agent messages, processing eventing, and handling callbacks).
   • Connect the backend to the database (Postgres) and also show real-time data flow to Hasura.
   • Show container orchestration via Docker Compose that brings together all of these elements.

3. Highlight the key architectural patterns and design principles:
   • Microservices/Service-Oriented Architecture: With separate containers/services for different functions (backend API, messaging, database, web UI).
   • Containerization and Orchestration: Docker and docker-compose support isolation and scaling.
   • Event-Driven Communication: Via RabbitMQ, where services consume and produce messages (controlled by custom RabbitMQ utilities in the “mythic-docker/src/rabbitmq” directory).
   • Modular and Extensible System: The separation of agents and C2 profiles (installed externally via GitHub) is an important extensibility point.
   • Multi-Tier Design: Separating user interface, business logic, and data layers.

4. Tailor the diagram to the Mythic project specifics:
   • Clearly separate the UI layer from the core backend services.
   • Emphasize the orchestration provided by Mythic_CLI, noting how the CLI is central to starting and updating components.
   • Indicate the integration between Go-based backend components (mythic-docker), the Python base containers, and the React UI.
   • Show the utilization of external services (like RabbitMQ, PostgreSQL, Hasura, nginx) as discrete, interacting modules.

5. Instructions for diagram elements:
   • Components/Modules: Use clear boxes for each component—label the UI, API/backend, messaging system, databases, external services, and CLI.
   • Directional Arrows: Draw arrows to show API calls (e.g., from UI to backend), event flows (from backend to RabbitMQ and then to agents), and configuration flows (from CLI to all containers).
   • Color Coding and Shapes: Use different color schemes or shapes (e.g., rectangles for services, cylinders for databases, parallelograms for the CLI tool) to distinguish types of components.
   • Annotations: Include notes on what technology each component uses (e.g., “React”, “Go”, “RabbitMQ”, “Postgres”, “Docker Container”) and any interdependencies.

6. Additional diagram details:
   • If needed, include sub-diagrams or insets for particularly complex components—such as more detailed views of the backend’s internal structure, the RabbitMQ message flows (one-to-one, one-to-many, tasking, eventing), or the container orchestration layout.
   • Emphasize that Mythic is modular—agents and C2 profiles are not included in the core code, but are installed and dynamically updated via the CLI. You might include them as “extensible modules” attached to the main backend service.
   • Make sure to label versioning and the boundary between core Mythic and externally developed components.

By following these guidelines, you’re able to produce a detailed, clear system design diagram that captures every essential architectural element—including services, communications, and technology stack—of the Mythic red teaming framework.
</explanation>
